prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- The fiery leader of Lebanon's Hezbollah militant movement assured Lebanon on Monday that his movement will cooperate in the country's political life. Supporters carry posters of Hezbollah chief Hassan Nasrallah. Hassan Nasrallah said: "We don't want to have control over Lebanon, or to have governance over Lebanon or to impose our ideas over the people of Lebanon, because we believe Lebanon to be a special and diverse country that needs the collaboration of everyone." Nasrallah spoke a day after Lebanon's parliament elected Michel Sleiman the country's president after a six-month vacancy in the position. Nasrallah, speaking at a packed stadium, told his followers: "I renew my appeal and invitation for a true national partnership with no eliminations or impositions. The national unity government is not the victory of the opposition against the pro-government. It is the victory of all Lebanese." He said Sleiman's election "renews the hope amongst the Lebanese people to a new era and a new start." "I must say that there are deep wounds from our side and theirs, we are both in front of two choices; either to expand the wounds and add salt to them or try to cure them for the sake of Lebanon and we prefer the second choice." The parliament had tried 19 times to vote on a new president, but failed because of disagreements over how to share power in a new Cabinet. Lebanon's Western-backed government and the Hezbollah-led opposition reached a deal last week aimed at ending an 18-month political crisis that pushed the country to the brink of civil war, and paved the way for Sleiman's election. The agreement, reached in Doha, Qatar, calls for a consensus government in which the Cabinet would be comprised of 30 posts -- 16 for the majority, 11 for the Hezbollah-led opposition and three set aside for the president to nominate. The seat allocation had been a key sticking point for the opposition, which wanted to ensure it had the power to veto major decisions. With 11 Cabinet posts, it will have that power. In exchange for the veto power and a redistricting plan ahead of next year's elections, Hezbollah agreed to end its sit-in protest that has paralyzed downtown Beirut since late 2006. In his speech, Sleiman expressed gratitude to Qatar and to the Arab League for helping broker the deal. Sleiman was the consensus candidate, and is viewed as a neutral party by Lebanon's political factions. The nation's previous presidents have been seen as either pro-Syrian or pro-Western. In his 10 years as chief of the army, Sleiman also is believed to have unified the splintered military. However, he inherits a nation grappling with divisions. Lebanon's elected, pro-Western government has long been locked in a power struggle with Hezbollah. In public statements and demonstrations in recent years, Hezbollah threatened to use its power and popularity to oust the Sunni-led government, triggering fears of a new civil war that could further destabilize the volatile region. The election helped end a political crisis that deteriorated into violence this month. That crisis was defused when the Lebanese government gave in to two key Hezbollah demands -- lifting a government ban of Hezbollah's telecommunications system and reinstating the chief of security at Beirut's airport. "The performance of the opposition proved that it did not organize a coup, but only wanted the illegal government to withdraw its two decisions," Nasrallah said. "I promise that the opposition's representation in the government will not be monopolized by Hezbollah, Amal and the Change and Reform bloc. We will give other opposition parties shares - and unfortunately we must speak of shares - even if it is at the expense of Hezbollah's shares." Hezbollah has been linked to numerous terrorist attacks against U.S., Israeli, and other Western targets and the United States lists it as a terrorist organization. But many in Lebanon and other parts of the Middle East -- particularly Shiites -- view Hezbollah militants as freedom fighters.

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) — The fiery leader of Lebanon’s Hezbollah militant movement assured Lebanon on Monday that his movement would cooperate in the country’s political life.

Supporters carried posters of Hezbollah chief Hassan Nasrallah.

“We don’t want to have control over Lebanon, or to have governance over Lebanon, or to impose our ideas on the people of Lebanon, because we believe Lebanon to be a special and diverse country that needs the collaboration of everyone,” Hassan Nasrallah said.

Nasrallah spoke a day after Lebanon’s parliament elected Michel Sleiman as the country’s president, ending a six-month vacancy in the post.

Speaking before a packed stadium, Nasrallah told his followers: “I renew my appeal and invitation for a true national partnership with no eliminations or impositions. The national unity government is not the victory of the opposition against the pro-government. It is the victory of all Lebanese.”

He said Sleiman’s election “renews the hope amongst the Lebanese people to a new era and a new start.”

“I must say that there are deep wounds from our side and theirs. We are both in front of two choices: either to expand the wounds and add salt to them, or try to cure them for the sake of Lebanon. We prefer the second choice.”

Parliament had tried 19 times to vote on a new president but failed because of disagreements over how to share power in a new Cabinet.

Lebanon’s Western-backed government and the Hezbollah-led opposition reached a deal last week aimed at ending an 18-month political crisis that had pushed the country to the brink of civil war and paved the way for Sleiman’s election.

The agreement, reached in Doha, Qatar, calls for a consensus government in which the Cabinet would comprise 30 posts: 16 for the majority, 11 for the Hezbollah-led opposition, and three set aside for the president to nominate.

The seat allocation had been a key sticking point for the opposition, which wanted to ensure it had the power to veto major decisions. With 11 Cabinet posts, it will have that power.

In exchange for the veto power and a redistricting plan ahead of next year’s elections, Hezbollah agreed to end its sit-in protest, which had paralyzed downtown Beirut since late 2006.

In his speech, Sleiman expressed gratitude to Qatar and to the Arab League for helping broker the deal.

Sleiman was the consensus candidate and is viewed as a neutral party by Lebanon’s political factions. The nation’s previous presidents have been seen as either pro-Syrian or pro-Western.

In his 10 years as army chief, Sleiman is also believed to have unified the splintered military.

However, he inherits a nation grappling with deep divisions. Lebanon’s elected, pro-Western government has long been locked in a power struggle with Hezbollah.

In public statements and demonstrations in recent years, Hezbollah threatened to use its power and popularity to oust the Sunni-led government, triggering fears of a new civil war that could further destabilize the volatile region.

The election helped end a political crisis that deteriorated into violence this month. That crisis was defused when the Lebanese government yielded to two key Hezbollah demands: lifting a government ban on Hezbollah’s telecommunications system and reinstating the chief of security at Beirut’s airport.

“The performance of the opposition proved that it did not organize a coup, but only wanted the illegal government to withdraw its two decisions,” Nasrallah said.

“I promise that the opposition’s representation in the government will not be monopolized by Hezbollah, Amal, and the Change and Reform bloc. We will give other opposition parties shares — and unfortunately we must speak of shares — even if it is at the expense of Hezbollah’s shares.”

Hezbollah has been linked to numerous terrorist attacks against U.S., Israeli, and other Western targets, and the United States lists it as a terrorist organization. However, many in Lebanon and other parts of the Middle East — particularly Shiites — view Hezbollah militants as freedom fighters.

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) — Hezbollah’s forceful leader, Hassan Nasrallah, told the Lebanese people on Monday that his movement would take part constructively in the country’s political process.

Supporters held up posters of Hezbollah chief Hassan Nasrallah.

Nasrallah said Hezbollah did not seek to dominate Lebanon, rule the country, or force its views on Lebanese citizens. He said the movement sees Lebanon as a unique and pluralistic nation that requires cooperation among all its communities.

His remarks came one day after Lebanon’s parliament chose Michel Sleiman as president, ending a six-month period in which the office had been vacant.

Speaking before a crowded stadium, Nasrallah addressed his supporters by calling again for what he described as a genuine national partnership, without exclusion or coercion. He said the formation of a national unity government should not be seen as a triumph by the opposition over the pro-government camp, but as a success for all Lebanese people.

Nasrallah said Sleiman’s election had restored hope among Lebanese citizens for a new phase and a fresh beginning. He added that both sides had suffered serious wounds and now faced two options: to deepen those wounds and inflame them further, or to try to heal them for Lebanon’s benefit. He said Hezbollah favored the second path.

Lebanon’s parliament had attempted 19 times to elect a new president, but each effort failed because of disputes over the division of power in a future Cabinet.

The Western-supported Lebanese government and the Hezbollah-led opposition reached an agreement the previous week intended to resolve an 18-month political standoff that had brought the country close to civil war and cleared the way for Sleiman’s election.

The deal, negotiated in Doha, Qatar, provides for a consensus government with a 30-member Cabinet. Under the arrangement, the majority would receive 16 seats, the Hezbollah-led opposition would receive 11, and the president would name three ministers.

The distribution of Cabinet seats had been one of the main obstacles for the opposition, which wanted enough representation to block major government decisions. With 11 seats, it will have that veto authority.

In return for obtaining veto power and an agreement on redrawing districts ahead of elections scheduled for the following year, Hezbollah agreed to end its sit-in protest, which had crippled central Beirut since late 2006.

In his own speech, Sleiman thanked Qatar and the Arab League for their role in mediating the agreement.

Sleiman was selected as a consensus figure and is regarded by Lebanon’s rival political groups as neutral. Earlier Lebanese presidents had generally been viewed as aligned either with Syria or with the West.

During his decade as army commander, Sleiman is also credited with helping bring together Lebanon’s fragmented military. Still, he assumes office in a country facing deep internal divisions.

Lebanon’s elected, pro-Western government had long been caught in a struggle for power with Hezbollah. In public remarks and street demonstrations over recent years, Hezbollah had warned that it could use its influence and popular support to remove the Sunni-led government, raising fears of another civil war that could add instability to an already tense region.

The presidential vote helped bring to a close a political crisis that had turned violent earlier in the month. The confrontation eased after the Lebanese government accepted two central Hezbollah demands: reversing a government ban on Hezbollah’s telecommunications network and reinstating the security chief at Beirut’s airport.

Nasrallah said the opposition’s conduct showed it had not been attempting a coup, but had only wanted what he called the illegal government to reverse those two decisions.

He also pledged that the opposition’s share in the government would not be controlled solely by Hezbollah, Amal, and the Change and Reform bloc. He said other opposition groups would be given portions of that representation — adding that, regrettably, the discussion had to be framed in terms of “shares” — even if doing so reduced Hezbollah’s own portion.

Hezbollah has been connected to numerous terrorist attacks targeting U.S., Israeli, and other Western interests, and Washington designates it as a terrorist organization. However, many people in Lebanon and elsewhere in the Middle East, especially Shiites, regard Hezbollah fighters as freedom fighters.

counterfactuals.output:
**Nasrallah says Hezbollah will cooperate after Sleiman elected Lebanese president**

**BEIRUT, Lebanon** — Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah sought to reassure Lebanese citizens that his movement would work through political channels following the election of Michel Sleiman as president and the signing of the Doha agreement, which ended months of political deadlock and street violence.

In a televised address after Sleiman’s election, Nasrallah said Hezbollah and its allies would cooperate with the new government formed under the terms of the Qatar-brokered deal. He described the agreement as an opportunity to restore stability and prevent Lebanon from sliding back into internal conflict.

The Doha accord, reached by Lebanon’s rival political factions, paved the way for parliament to elect Sleiman, the former army commander, as president after the office had remained vacant for months. The agreement also called for the formation of a national unity government and a new electoral law.

Nasrallah told Lebanese citizens that Hezbollah’s participation in government would be political and institutional, stressing the need for dialogue among the country’s competing sectarian and political blocs. His comments appeared aimed at easing fears after deadly clashes earlier in May between Hezbollah-led opposition supporters and groups aligned with the Western-backed governing coalition.

Those confrontations, some of the worst internal fighting since Lebanon’s civil war, erupted after the government moved against Hezbollah’s private communications network and sought to remove the head of security at Beirut’s airport, a figure seen as close to the group. Hezbollah called the government’s decisions a threat to its resistance against Israel and responded by briefly taking control of parts of west Beirut.

The crisis raised concerns that Lebanon could face a prolonged armed confrontation, but Arab mediation in Doha brought the factions to an agreement. Sleiman’s election was widely welcomed by regional and international leaders as a step toward ending the standoff.

Nasrallah said Hezbollah would support efforts to rebuild trust and keep disputes inside constitutional institutions. But he also reiterated the group’s position that its weapons remain tied to its conflict with Israel, an issue that continues to divide Lebanon’s political class.

Sleiman, in his inaugural remarks, called for national unity and dialogue over Hezbollah’s arms, while pledging to strengthen state institutions and preserve Lebanon’s fragile stability.

The coming weeks are expected to test whether the Doha agreement can hold, as Lebanon’s leaders negotiate the makeup of the unity government and prepare for parliamentary elections.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a detailed news report from Beirut on Lebanon’s 2008 political crisis, including Hezbollah’s reaction, Nasrallah’s speech, the national unity government deal, and Michel Sleiman’s presidency.
counterfactuals.output:
**Beirut —** Lebanon’s long-running political crisis reached its most dangerous point in May 2008, when a confrontation between the Western-backed government and the Hezbollah-led opposition erupted into street battles, armed takeovers, and a near-collapse of the state before Arab mediation produced a power-sharing deal and cleared the way for the election of army commander Michel Sleiman as president.

The crisis had been building since late 2006, when Hezbollah and its allies withdrew from the cabinet and launched a sit-in in central Beirut, accusing Prime Minister Fouad Siniora’s government of ruling without sufficient Shiite representation and of aligning too closely with the United States and Saudi Arabia. The governing March 14 coalition, which had emerged after the 2005 assassination of former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri and the withdrawal of Syrian troops, accused Hezbollah of acting as an armed state within the state and of serving Iranian and Syrian interests.

The standoff paralyzed political life for roughly 18 months. Parliament was repeatedly unable to elect a successor to President Émile Lahoud after his term expired in November 2007, leaving the presidency vacant. The army, led by Gen. Michel Sleiman, became one of the few institutions still seen as capable of preventing total breakdown.

## Government moves ignite confrontation

The immediate trigger came in early May 2008, when Siniora’s cabinet announced measures targeting Hezbollah’s private telecommunications network and the head of security at Beirut’s international airport, Brig. Gen. Wafiq Shuqair, who was accused by government allies of being close to Hezbollah.

The cabinet declared Hezbollah’s independent communications network illegal and said it would refer the matter to judicial authorities. The network had long been a point of contention. Hezbollah argued it was an essential part of its resistance infrastructure against Israel, particularly after the 2006 war. The government and its March 14 supporters said it undermined Lebanese sovereignty and represented a parallel security apparatus outside state control.

The decision was received by Hezbollah as an existential challenge. The movement’s supporters and allied opposition groups quickly escalated protests. Roads were blocked, including routes to Beirut airport, and tensions spread through the capital.

## Hezbollah’s reaction and Nasrallah’s speech

Hezbollah Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah responded with one of the most consequential speeches of the crisis. Speaking by video link, Nasrallah denounced the cabinet’s decisions as a direct attack on the “resistance” and said the move against the telecommunications network amounted to a “declaration of war.”

He argued that the network was not a political tool but a defensive weapon used to protect Lebanon from Israeli intelligence and military operations. Nasrallah accused the government of attempting to strip Hezbollah of its capacity to resist Israel and of taking orders from foreign powers, especially the United States.

His message was stark: Hezbollah would not allow the dismantling of its communications system. The group, he said, would respond to those trying to target its weapons and infrastructure. The speech signaled that Hezbollah saw the confrontation not as a cabinet dispute but as a red line over its military independence.

Within hours, fighting intensified.

## Armed clashes in Beirut and beyond

Hezbollah fighters and allied Amal movement gunmen moved through mainly Sunni neighborhoods of West Beirut, where supporters of the March 14 coalition and the Future Movement of Saad Hariri were based. After fierce clashes, opposition gunmen took control of much of West Beirut, including offices and media outlets linked to the Future Movement.

The takeover stunned Lebanon. It was the first time Hezbollah had turned its weapons so visibly inward on the Lebanese political scene, contradicting its longstanding claim that its arms were reserved for resistance against Israel. March 14 leaders accused the group of staging an armed coup. Hezbollah and its allies said they had acted defensively against a government that had crossed a line.

Violence also spread to the Chouf mountains and other mixed areas, raising fears of a renewed civil war. Dozens of people were killed in several days of fighting. The Lebanese army deployed but largely avoided direct confrontation with Hezbollah, a decision that was criticized by some government supporters but defended by others as necessary to prevent the army from splitting along sectarian lines.

Under pressure, the cabinet later reversed or suspended the disputed decisions regarding Hezbollah’s communications network and the airport security chief, easing the immediate trigger for the fighting but not resolving the underlying political deadlock.

## Arab mediation and the Doha agreement

With Lebanon on the brink, the Arab League intervened, dispatching mediators and pushing rival leaders into talks in Doha, Qatar. The negotiations brought together figures from the March 14 majority and the Hezbollah-led March 8 opposition.

After days of intense bargaining, the parties reached the **Doha Agreement** on May 21, 2008. The deal ended the immediate crisis and laid out a roadmap for restoring state institutions.

Its key elements included:

- **Election of Michel Sleiman as president**, ending the six-month presidential vacuum.
- **Formation of a national unity government** of 30 ministers.
- A cabinet formula giving the March 14 majority 16 ministers, the opposition 11 ministers, and the president 3 ministers.
- The opposition’s 11 seats effectively gave it veto power over major cabinet decisions, a central demand of Hezbollah and its allies.
- Agreement on a new electoral law, largely based on the 1960 framework, for the 2009 parliamentary elections.
- A pledge by all sides to refrain from using weapons or violence for political gains.

The deal was hailed by Arab mediators as a rescue package for Lebanon, though many Lebanese saw it as a compromise born of force. March 14 retained formal parliamentary majority status, but the opposition secured the “blocking third” it had long demanded.

## National unity government deal

The national unity government was designed to contain the crisis by bringing Lebanon’s rival blocs into a single cabinet. Under the 16-11-3 arrangement, the majority could not govern alone, and the opposition could not topple the cabinet by itself without additional support. The president’s three ministers were meant to serve as a balancing element.

For Hezbollah, the arrangement was a political victory. It preserved the group’s weapons and communications network from immediate state action and granted its camp institutional veto power. For March 14, the agreement prevented further bloodshed, restored the presidency, and kept the country on track for elections, though at the cost of major concessions.

The unity cabinet later faced the familiar Lebanese challenge: balancing government authority with Hezbollah’s independent military and security role. The Doha Agreement did not resolve the question of Hezbollah’s arms; it postponed it under the framework of future national dialogue.

## Michel Sleiman elected president

On May 25, 2008, Lebanon’s parliament elected **Michel Sleiman** president, filling the post that had been vacant since Lahoud’s departure. Sleiman, the commander of the Lebanese Armed Forces, was widely viewed as a compromise candidate acceptable to both the March 14 coalition and the Hezbollah-led opposition.

His election was attended by regional and international dignitaries and was presented as a moment of national recovery after weeks of fear. In his inaugural address, Sleiman called for dialogue, national unity, and a defense strategy that would address the role of Hezbollah’s weapons within the Lebanese state. He also emphasized the need to strengthen the army and preserve civil peace.

Sleiman’s presidency symbolized the return of constitutional order, but it also reflected the limits of state power. The events of May 2008 had shown that Lebanon’s political system remained deeply vulnerable to sectarian division, regional rivalry, and the unresolved status of Hezbollah’s armed wing.

## A fragile calm

The 2008 crisis left a lasting mark on Lebanon. Hezbollah emerged militarily dominant on the ground and politically strengthened in the cabinet. March 14 survived as the parliamentary majority but with reduced leverage. The Lebanese army maintained cohesion but at the price of avoiding confrontation with the most powerful armed faction in the country.

The Doha Agreement restored a measure of stability, but it did not settle the central dispute over sovereignty and arms. Instead, it institutionalized a temporary balance: no side could rule alone, and no side could be easily defeated.

From Beirut, the lesson of the crisis was clear. Lebanon had avoided a return to full-scale civil war, but only through a fragile compromise that left the country’s deepest conflicts unresolved.

Sleiman’s election followed an Arab-brokered agreement in Doha between the Western-backed governing coalition and the Hezbollah-led opposition. The deal came after days of street fighting in Beirut and other areas, triggered by government moves against Hezbollah’s communications network and a senior airport security official. Hezbollah and its allies briefly seized control of parts of west Beirut before the sides agreed to negotiations.

Under the settlement, Sleiman was chosen as a consensus president, a national unity government was to be formed, and a new electoral law adopted ahead of parliamentary polls. The agreement gave the opposition effective veto power in the cabinet, addressing one of Hezbollah’s central demands.

Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah welcomed the political breakthrough but said Lebanon could not be governed by one camp alone. In remarks following the agreement, he stressed the need for “national partnership” and said no Lebanese faction could exclude or eliminate another.

Nasrallah also defended Hezbollah’s actions during the crisis, saying the group’s weapons were not aimed at imposing domestic rule but at protecting what it calls the resistance against Israel. His comments reflected the central dispute in Lebanese politics: whether Hezbollah’s armed wing should remain outside state control or be integrated into a national defense framework.

Sleiman’s election was widely seen as a temporary stabilization measure after months of institutional paralysis. But diplomats and analysts said the underlying divisions — over Hezbollah’s weapons, power-sharing, and Lebanon’s regional alignments — remained unresolved.

# How the Doha Agreement Ended Lebanon’s Presidential Deadlock — and What Hezbollah Gained

In May 2008, Lebanon’s long-running political crisis reached a breaking point. After months of institutional paralysis, a vacant presidency, and an escalating confrontation between the Western- and Saudi-backed March 14 coalition and the Hezbollah-led opposition, fighting erupted in Beirut and other areas. The violence shocked Lebanon and alarmed regional powers. It also created the conditions for a rapid diplomatic intervention by Qatar, which hosted Lebanese leaders in Doha and brokered an agreement that ended the immediate crisis.

The resulting Doha Agreement, announced on May 21, 2008, paved the way for the election of army commander Michel Suleiman as president, created a national unity government, and gave Hezbollah and its allies the Cabinet leverage they had demanded for more than a year. Publicly, Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah framed the deal as a political settlement that prevented civil war, protected the “Resistance,” and corrected what he portrayed as an attempt by his rivals to marginalize the opposition.

## Background: Lebanon’s Presidential Vacuum

Lebanon had been without a president since November 2007, when President Émile Lahoud’s term ended. Under Lebanon’s sectarian power-sharing system, the presidency is reserved for a Maronite Christian, the premiership for a Sunni Muslim, and the speakership of parliament for a Shiite Muslim.

The leading candidate to succeed Lahoud was General Michel Suleiman, the commander of the Lebanese Armed Forces. He was widely seen as a compromise figure acceptable to both the March 14 majority and the Hezbollah-led opposition. Yet his election was repeatedly delayed because the presidency was tied to a broader struggle over executive power, Cabinet composition, and electoral rules.

The March 14 coalition, which had emerged after the 2005 assassination of former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri and the withdrawal of Syrian troops from Lebanon, held a parliamentary majority. It included Saad Hariri’s Future Movement, Walid Jumblatt’s Progressive Socialist Party, and the Lebanese Forces, among others. It was broadly aligned with the United States, France, and Saudi Arabia.

Opposing it was the March 8 camp, led by Hezbollah and the Amal Movement, and including Michel Aoun’s Free Patriotic Movement. This bloc was aligned more closely with Syria and Iran and demanded a greater share of power in government. Its central demand was a “blocking third” in Cabinet — enough ministers to veto major decisions or bring down the government by resigning.

For the March 14 camp, granting that demand would have allowed Hezbollah and its allies to paralyze the government from within. For Hezbollah, the demand was presented as necessary protection against unilateral decisions by a hostile majority, especially decisions affecting its weapons, communications network, and military capacity.

## The Immediate Trigger: May 2008 Confrontation

The crisis turned violent in early May 2008 after the Lebanese government took two decisions aimed at Hezbollah.

First, the government declared Hezbollah’s private telecommunications network illegal. Hezbollah considered that network a core component of its military infrastructure against Israel. Second, the government moved against the head of airport security, Brig. Gen. Wafiq Shuqeir, who was considered close to Hezbollah, after allegations that Hezbollah had installed surveillance equipment near Beirut airport.

Hezbollah interpreted these decisions as a declaration of war against the Resistance. Nasrallah said the communications network was essential to Hezbollah’s ability to defend Lebanon from Israel and that any attempt to dismantle it crossed a red line.

Armed clashes followed. Hezbollah and allied fighters moved into parts of West Beirut, overwhelming pro-government gunmen. Fighting also spread to other areas, including the mountains. The violence left dozens dead and raised fears that Lebanon was sliding back toward civil war.

The March 14 coalition accused Hezbollah of staging an armed coup against the Lebanese state. Hezbollah rejected that characterization, insisting that it had acted defensively to stop government decisions that threatened the Resistance.

## Qatar’s Mediation and the Doha Talks

With the situation deteriorating, the Arab League intervened, and Qatar took the lead in hosting negotiations among Lebanon’s rival factions. Qatari diplomacy was well placed for the task: Doha had maintained working relations with a wide range of regional actors, including Syria, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Western governments, and Lebanese factions.

Lebanese leaders traveled to Doha for intensive talks. The negotiations focused on three core issues:

1. The election of a president  
2. The formation of a national unity government  
3. A new parliamentary election law  

The talks also addressed the immediate security crisis and the need to prevent the use of weapons in domestic political disputes.

The breakthrough came with a package deal that allowed each side to claim something. March 14 got the election of Michel Suleiman and a path back to institutional normalcy. Hezbollah and its allies got the Cabinet blocking power they had demanded. Christian factions, especially Michel Aoun’s Free Patriotic Movement, got changes to the electoral law that improved their prospects in future parliamentary elections.

## Ending the Presidential Deadlock: Michel Suleiman’s Election

The most immediate effect of the Doha Agreement was to end the presidential vacuum.

The agreement committed Lebanon’s parliament to convene and elect General Michel Suleiman as president. On May 25, 2008, just days after the accord, parliament elected Suleiman, filling the office that had been vacant for roughly six months.

Suleiman’s election was significant because it restored the top office in Lebanon’s confessional system and provided a constitutional anchor for the next phase of government formation. He was viewed as a compromise figure because, as army commander, he had avoided direct alignment with either camp during the political crisis. The army had largely stayed out of the May fighting, a stance that preserved its national image but also reflected the danger of splitting the military along sectarian lines.

By agreeing to Suleiman, both camps accepted a president who was neither an outright March 14 figure nor a Hezbollah loyalist. His election was therefore the mechanism through which the Doha Agreement translated political compromise into institutional action.

## The Cabinet Concessions Hezbollah Received

The most important concession Hezbollah and its allies received was in the composition of the new national unity Cabinet.

Under the Doha Agreement, the Cabinet would have 30 ministers, divided as follows:

- 16 ministers for the March 14 parliamentary majority  
- 11 ministers for the opposition, including Hezbollah and its allies  
- 3 ministers appointed by the president  

This formula was crucial because 11 seats in a 30-member Cabinet gave the opposition more than one-third of the government. In Lebanese politics, that “blocking third” — sometimes called the “veto third” — is a powerful tool. It allows a bloc to block major Cabinet decisions requiring a two-thirds majority. It can also potentially bring down the government if its ministers resign collectively.

For Hezbollah, this was the central political prize of Doha.

The opposition had withdrawn its ministers from the government of Prime Minister Fouad Siniora in 2006 and had spent months demanding a national unity government in which it would hold veto power. The March 14 coalition had resisted, arguing that Hezbollah was trying to override the results of the 2005 parliamentary elections. Doha resolved the confrontation by giving Hezbollah’s camp the leverage it wanted.

The agreement also stipulated that no side would resign or obstruct government functioning, but in practical terms the opposition had gained the institutional safeguard it sought. It could now prevent the Cabinet from taking major decisions against Hezbollah’s strategic interests, especially on the issue of its arms and security infrastructure.

## Why the Blocking Third Mattered

Hezbollah’s military wing and its weapons had long been one of Lebanon’s most contentious issues. March 14 leaders argued that no party should maintain an independent armed force outside the authority of the state. Hezbollah argued that its weapons were necessary to resist Israel and defend Lebanon, especially after the 2006 Lebanon War.

The Cabinet confrontation in May 2008 showed why Hezbollah cared so much about veto power. The government’s decisions on the telecommunications network and airport security were, in Hezbollah’s view, exactly the sort of moves that a blocking third could prevent.

With 11 ministers, Hezbollah and its allies did not need to control the whole government. They simply needed enough power to stop decisions they considered existential threats. Doha gave them that.

The concession therefore did not formally legalize Hezbollah’s weapons, nor did it settle Lebanon’s defense strategy. But it ensured that any future government decision targeting Hezbollah’s military infrastructure would be extremely difficult without opposition consent.

## The Electoral Law Compromise

In addition to the presidency and Cabinet formula, the Doha Agreement included a compromise on the parliamentary election law.

The parties agreed to use a modified version of the 1960 electoral law for the 2009 parliamentary elections. This law relied on smaller electoral districts, known as qada-level districts, rather than larger governorate-level districts.

This mattered particularly to Christian parties. Michel Aoun’s Free Patriotic Movement had argued that smaller districts would allow Christian voters to elect more of their own representatives rather than having Christian seats determined by Muslim-majority districts. The March 14 Christian parties also had an interest in districting, but Aoun’s camp saw the 1960 law as a major gain.

For Hezbollah, the electoral law was less central than the Cabinet formula, but it helped secure the support of its Christian ally, Aoun. The Doha package thus reinforced the broader March 8 alliance.

## The Agreement on Weapons and Internal Conflict

The Doha Agreement also included language emphasizing that weapons should not be used to achieve political gains inside Lebanon. This clause was designed to address the trauma of the May clashes and reassure the March 14 camp that Hezbollah’s armed takeover of parts of Beirut would not become a recurring tactic.

However, the agreement did not directly disarm Hezbollah or place its weapons under state control. Nor did it create an enforceable mechanism to do so. Instead, it called for renewed national dialogue on Lebanon’s security and defense strategy.

This was another important point for Hezbollah. The agreement condemned the use of weapons in internal disputes in general terms, but it did not treat Hezbollah’s arsenal as illegitimate. It left the question of the Resistance’s arms to future dialogue — a forum in which Hezbollah could defend its position politically while maintaining its military capabilities.

## How Nasrallah Framed the Deal Publicly

Hassan Nasrallah presented the Doha Agreement as a victory for political partnership, national stability, and the protection of the Resistance.

He did not frame it as a coup, despite Hezbollah’s rapid military success in Beirut. Instead, he argued that Hezbollah had been forced to respond to government actions that threatened its ability to resist Israel. In his public messaging, the May events were not an attempt to seize power but a defensive move against decisions he described as dangerous and illegitimate.

Nasrallah emphasized several themes.

### 1. “No victor and no vanquished”

One of the most important public frames was the idea that the agreement should not be understood as one side defeating the other. Lebanese political discourse often invokes the phrase “no victor, no vanquished,” especially after internal crises. Nasrallah used this kind of language to present the settlement as a national compromise rather than a triumphalist conquest.

This framing served a political purpose. Hezbollah had demonstrated its military superiority on the ground, but openly celebrating a domestic military victory risked deepening sectarian resentment, especially among Sunnis who saw the Beirut fighting as a humiliation. By speaking in terms of compromise, Nasrallah sought to reduce the appearance that Hezbollah had imposed the agreement by force.

### 2. Defense of the Resistance

Nasrallah also framed the deal as a protection of the Resistance. He argued that Hezbollah’s communications network and weapons were not internal political tools but essential elements in the struggle against Israel. The government’s attempt to move against the network was, in his telling, an attack on Lebanon’s defensive capacity.

The Doha outcome allowed him to say that the Resistance had been safeguarded. The agreement did not dismantle Hezbollah’s military infrastructure, did not disarm the group, and did not empower the Cabinet to act against it without opposition consent.

### 3. Restoration of partnership

Nasrallah portrayed the Cabinet formula as a correction to political exclusion. From Hezbollah’s perspective, the March 14 majority had governed unilaterally and ignored the concerns of a major segment of the Lebanese population, particularly the Shiite community and Hezbollah’s allies.

By winning the blocking third, the opposition could claim that Lebanon’s consensus-based system had been restored. Nasrallah argued that major national decisions should not be made by a simple parliamentary majority when they affected fundamental questions of sovereignty, security, and communal balance.

### 4. Rejection of the coup accusation

March 14 leaders accused Hezbollah of using its arms internally and staging a coup against the state. Nasrallah rejected this. He insisted that Hezbollah did not seek to rule Lebanon, overthrow the government, or impose an Islamic state. He argued that if Hezbollah had wanted to take power militarily, it could have done far more than it did.

His message was that Hezbollah’s military action was limited, defensive, and aimed at reversing specific government decisions, not at capturing the Lebanese state.

### 5. Commitment to calm — on Hezbollah’s terms

Nasrallah welcomed the agreement as a way to end street confrontation and restore calm. But that calm rested on the new balance of power created by Doha: Hezbollah’s weapons remained untouched, and its political camp had gained veto power in Cabinet.

In effect, Nasrallah framed peace as possible once the opposition’s red lines were recognized.

## March 14’s Interpretation: A Settlement Under Pressure

For the March 14 coalition, the Doha Agreement was more ambiguous. On one hand, it ended the fighting, restored the presidency, and prevented a slide into civil war. On the other hand, many March 14 figures believed the agreement rewarded Hezbollah for using force.

The Cabinet formula was especially controversial. March 14 had won the 2005 parliamentary elections, yet Doha forced it to share executive power with an opposition bloc able to veto major decisions. Critics argued that the agreement weakened democratic majority rule and confirmed that Hezbollah’s weapons gave it leverage beyond its parliamentary weight.

Still, March 14 accepted the agreement because the alternative was continued paralysis and possible civil conflict. The election of Suleiman and the restoration of state institutions were seen as necessary, even at a high political cost.

## Regional Significance

The Doha Agreement also reflected wider regional dynamics. Lebanon’s internal politics were deeply connected to competition among Saudi Arabia, Syria, Iran, the United States, and France.

Hezbollah’s gains were widely viewed as a boost for the Syrian-Iranian axis. The March 14 coalition had tried to consolidate Lebanese sovereignty after Syria’s 2005 withdrawal, but the 2008 crisis showed that Hezbollah remained the most powerful armed actor in the country.

Qatar’s role enhanced its regional diplomatic profile. By bringing the factions to agreement, Doha positioned itself as a mediator capable of speaking to all sides.

## What the Agreement Solved — and What It Did Not

The Doha Agreement solved Lebanon’s immediate institutional crisis. It ended the presidential vacuum, produced a national unity government, and set the rules for the 2009 elections.

But it did not resolve the underlying conflict over Hezbollah’s weapons, the authority of the Lebanese state, or the relationship between majority rule and consensus politics. Instead, it froze those disputes into a new political arrangement.

Hezbollah emerged with its core assets intact: its arms, its communications infrastructure, its alliance network, and now a Cabinet veto. March 14 retained a formal majority but lost the ability to govern without opposition consent on major issues.

The agreement therefore stabilized Lebanon in the short term while institutionalizing a balance of power shaped by Hezbollah’s military and political strength.

## Conclusion

The Doha-brokered agreement ended Lebanon’s presidential deadlock by creating a comprehensive bargain: Michel Suleiman would be elected president, a national unity Cabinet would be formed, and parliamentary elections would proceed under a revised version of the 1960 law.

The key Cabinet concession to Hezbollah and its allies was the granting of 11 out of 30 ministerial seats — the long-sought blocking third. This gave the opposition veto power over major government decisions and protected Hezbollah from unilateral Cabinet moves against its military infrastructure.

Hassan Nasrallah publicly framed the deal not as a coup or a sectarian victory, but as a national compromise that prevented civil war, restored political partnership, and protected the Resistance. Yet the balance of the agreement was clear: Hezbollah had used a moment of crisis to secure the political veto it had demanded, while Lebanon’s unresolved debate over arms, sovereignty, and state authority was postponed rather than settled.

counterfactuals.output:
BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah pledged Monday that his Shiite militant and political movement would not seek to dominate Lebanon, a day after parliament elected army commander Michel Sleiman as president, ending a months-long political vacuum.

In a televised address, Nasrallah said Hezbollah’s goal was not to take control of the Lebanese state but to protect what it calls the “resistance” against Israel.

“We do not want power over Lebanon,” Nasrallah said, adding that the group sought partnership in government rather than control. He said the election of Sleiman opened the door to a new phase of political cooperation after weeks of violence and paralysis.

Sleiman was elected Sunday by Lebanon’s parliament after a deal brokered in Doha, Qatar, between the Western-backed governing coalition and the Hezbollah-led opposition. The agreement ended an 18-month political standoff and followed street battles in Beirut and other areas that raised fears of a return to civil war.

The new president, a consensus figure who led Lebanon’s army since 1998, called in his inaugural address for national unity and dialogue over Hezbollah’s weapons, one of the country’s most divisive issues.

Nasrallah defended Hezbollah’s brief takeover of parts of west Beirut earlier this month, saying the group acted after the government moved against its private telecommunications network and removed the airport security chief, who was seen as close to Hezbollah.

The fighting left dozens dead and marked the worst internal violence in Lebanon since the 1975-1990 civil war.

Under the Doha agreement, the opposition is to receive enough Cabinet seats to wield veto power, while rival factions also agreed on a new electoral law and the formation of a national unity government.

Lebanon had been without a president since Emile Lahoud’s term ended in November. Repeated attempts to elect a successor collapsed amid disputes between the governing coalition and the opposition.

Sleiman’s election was welcomed by regional and international leaders as a step toward restoring stability in a country long caught in the competing influence of Syria, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the West.

But major challenges remain, including the role of Hezbollah’s armed wing, relations with Syria, economic strains and deep sectarian mistrust.

Nasrallah said Hezbollah was ready for dialogue but insisted that any discussion of its arms must take place within a broader national defense strategy.
